```{r setup}
## Render from the project folder after a run of validation/run_all.R:
##   quarto render validation/report.qmd
## The checks are read from the run's logs (cache/logs/), the outcome table
## from study 06's cache; the figures are validation/results/figures/.
library(knitr)
project <- if (file.exists("DESCRIPTION")) normalizePath(".") else normalizePath("..")
figure <- function(name) include_graphics(file.path(project, "validation", "results", "figures",
                                                    paste0(name, ".png")))
check_lines <- function(study) {
  log_file <- file.path(project, "cache", "logs", paste0(study, ".log"))
  if (!file.exists(log_file)) return(character(0))
  grep("^\\[(PASS|FAIL)\\]", readLines(log_file, warn = FALSE, encoding = "UTF-8"), value = TRUE)
}
checks_of <- function(study) {
  lines <- check_lines(study)
  if (!length(lines)) return(data.frame(Note = "no pass/fail checks (a comparison study), or no log"))
  data.frame(Result = sub("^\\[(PASS|FAIL)\\].*", "\\1", lines),
             Check = trimws(gsub("\\s{2,}", " | ", sub("^\\[(PASS|FAIL)\\] ", "", lines))))
}
summary_lines <- readLines(file.path(project, "validation", "results", "run_summary.md"),
                           encoding = "UTF-8")
run_line <- function(field)
  trimws(sub(".*\\*\\*:? *", "", grep(paste0("\\*\\*", field), summary_lines, value = TRUE)[1]))
studies <- c("01_prior_and_posterior", "02_bayes_factor", "03_simulations",
             "04_matched_comparison", "05_conditional_test", "06_broad_simulation", "07_estimation",
             "08_growing_k", "09_variable_selection", "10_calibration", "11_factor_terms")
counts <- t(sapply(studies, function(s) {
  l <- check_lines(s)
  c(passed = sum(startsWith(l, "[PASS]")), failed = sum(startsWith(l, "[FAIL]")))
}))
```

::: {.callout-note appearance="minimal"}
**Abstract.** With one predictor, the natural objective prior for testing a
regression coefficient is flat on its correlation. With several predictors,
valid correlation matrices force a choice of what stays flat as predictors
are added: each partial correlation, the multiple correlation *R*, or *R*².
The three choices form one family, in which *R*² follows a Beta(*a*, 1)
distribution with *a* = *k*/2, ½ or 1. We implemented all three with exact
Bayes factors and a Stan model and tested them side by side against the
criteria of Bayarri et al. (2012), simulation-based calibration, operating
characteristics and coherence with the joint model; `r sum(counts[, "passed"])`
of `r sum(counts)` checks passed. All three priors are computed correctly and
meet the formal criteria, but they behave differently. Under flat *R* and flat
*R*², the test of one coefficient drifts as other predictors are added, and
it does not become more accurate as it does so. At 20 predictors all
three tests rank datasets identically (AUC = .701), yet flat *R* leaves 92% of
true nulls undecided, whereas flat partial *r* confirms 88%. Only the
conditional test under flat partial *r* is the Bayes factor of one joint
model; under flat *R* the corresponding restricted model is not a proper
model. We recommend flat partial *r* and state its costs.
:::

# Introduction

Default ("objective") Bayes factors are widely used to test whether one
predictor matters in a regression, for instance through the JZS prior in the
BayesFactor package and in JASP. A default prior is meant to express nothing
beyond what is possible. With one predictor, the obvious choice is Jeffreys'
prior, which is flat on the correlation. With *k* predictors there is no
single obvious choice, and the choice has a consequence that is easy to miss.
It determines whether the evidence about one coefficient depends on how many
*other* predictors are in the model.

This report asks which of three candidate defaults should be used. It answers
the question by testing all three on equal terms.

# Methods

## Three priors, one family

Not every correlation-based quantity can be flat at once. Study 00 shows
this by drawing random valid correlation matrices of (*y*, *x*₁ … *x*ₖ). If
each **partial correlation** (= the correlation of *y* with one predictor after
removing the other predictors from both) is kept flat, *R*² grows with *k*. If *R* or *R*² is kept
flat, each partial correlation shrinks with *k*. The three versions define the
three priors compared here.

| Prior | *R*² prior | What stays flat as predictors are added | Known as |
|---|---|---|---|
| flat partial r | Beta(*k*/2, 1) | each partial correlation | LKJ(1); `stan_lm` with η = 1 |
| flat R | Beta(½, 1) | the multiple correlation *R* | — |
| flat R-squared | Beta(1, 1) | *R*² | — |

For every *k*, each simulated version is flat on its own scale (study 00,
checks F1–F3, 200,000 matrices per *k*). All three priors spread the total
explained variance in a uniformly random direction over the predictors (so one
predictor's share follows Beta(½, (*k* − 1)/2)), and all three are mixtures of
Zellner *g*-priors (Liang et al., 2008).

```{r}
#| fig-cap: "Study 00. What valid correlation matrices force, per k: the three versions share the matrices and differ only in what is kept flat."
include_graphics(file.path(project, "docs", "figures", "motivation_partial_r_R_R2_by_k.png"))
```

## Tests

Two tests of one coefficient are compared. The **conditional test** (= the
test of the coefficient's partial correlation against zero, using the prior
that the joint prior implies for it) looks at that coefficient alone. The
**joint test** compares the model with the predictor against the model
without it. JZS (Cauchy prior with scale 0.354) and Zellner–Siow (scale 1)
serve as reference methods.

The behaviour of the test is studied mainly in study 06. It crosses 72
designs: *k* = 2, 5, 10 or 20 predictors; *n* = 50, 200 or 1,000; predictor
correlations of 0, .30 or .70; and the other coefficients either sparse (one
of them 0.3, the rest zero) or dense (all 0.1). In each design the tested
coefficient *x*₁ has a true slope of 0, 0.1 or 0.2, with 200 datasets per
cell. Predictors have unit variance and the noise has standard deviation 1,
so a slope of 0.1 is a change of 0.1 noise standard deviations per standard
deviation of the predictor.

## Validation

The validation consists of twelve studies. Each study's criteria are fixed in
its script before it runs:

| Question | Criterion and source | Studies |
|---|---|---|
| Is it computed correctly? | Bayes factors against `integrate()`, brute-force sampling and a second derivation; Stan prior draws (KS); simulation-based calibration (Talts et al., 2018) | 01, 02, 05 |
| Does it meet the default-prior criteria? | Predictive matching, invariance, information, model-selection and intrinsic consistency (Bayarri et al., 2012) | 02, 08 |
| How does the test of one coefficient behave? | Discrimination (AUC) and what each test says at BF 3 (Schönbrodt & Wagenmakers, 2018) | 03, 04, 06, 11 |
| Is it calibrated and coherent? | Calibration on its own prior (Schad et al., 2023); the conditional test against the Savage–Dickey ratio of the joint model (Wagenmakers et al., 2010) | 10 |
| What does it cost for estimation and selection? | Prediction error, bias and coverage; variable selection | 07, 09 |

The run reported here started `r run_line("started")` (commit
`r sub(" (with uncommitted changes)", " (the uncommitted changes were to the documentation only)", run_line("commit"), fixed = TRUE)`; `r run_line("R")`; CmdStan `r run_line("CmdStan")`).
Every parallel task draws from its own random stream, so the results are the
same on any number of cores.

# Results

## All three are correct and meet the formal criteria

```{r}
kable(data.frame(Study = gsub("_", " ", rownames(counts)), Passed = counts[, "passed"],
                 Failed = counts[, "failed"], row.names = NULL),
      caption = "Checks per study, read from the run's logs (studies without checks are comparisons).")
```

All three priors pass every correctness check, and all three meet every
Bayarri et al. (2012) criterion that was checked: predictive matching at
*n* = *k* + 1, invariance, information consistency from *n* = *k* + 3,
model-selection consistency for fixed and growing *k*, and intrinsic
consistency. These criteria are checked numerically in the settings the
studies cover; none is proven analytically here. The closest result is the
calibration check for the noise standard deviation under flat partial *r*
(χ² *p* = .020, against a threshold of .01). In a separate diagnostic of the
same setting, the package's Stan model had no divergent transitions in 1,200
calibration fits. The one failed check (study 10, P4) is a property of flat
*R*², discussed in @sec-coherence.

## The test of one coefficient drifts with *k*, without becoming more accurate {#sec-drift}

The three conditional tests are equally accurate, and they differ only in
where they decide. Across the 72 designs of study 06, they separate true nulls from small
effects (slope 0.1) equally well: at each *k* the three areas under the ROC
curve (AUC) are identical (.728 at *k* = 2, .701 at *k* = 20), against .713
and .684 for JZS. At a
Bayes factor of 3, each test either supports the null (BF₀₁ > 3), supports an
effect (BF₁₀ > 3), or remains undecided:

```{r}
#| fig-cap: "Study 06. What each test says about x1 at BF 3, by k and the true slope. Top row: the truth is null, so purple is correct; lower rows: brown is correct."
figure("06_outcomes")
```

```{r}
outcomes_file <- file.path(project, "cache", "sim_broad.rds")
if (file.exists(outcomes_file)) {
  runs <- readRDS(outcomes_file)
  runs <- runs[runs$number_of_predictors == 20 & grepl("conditional|JZS", runs$method), ]
  runs$outcome <- ifelse(runs$log_BF10 < -log(3), "says null",
                         ifelse(runs$log_BF10 > log(3), "says effect", "undecided"))
  shares <- as.data.frame.matrix(prop.table(
    table(factor(paste(runs$method, "| slope", runs$slope_of_x1),
                 levels = paste(rep(c("flat partial r conditional", "flat R conditional",
                                      "flat R-squared conditional", "JZS default"), each = 3),
                                "| slope", c(0, 0.1, 0.2))),
          factor(runs$outcome, levels = c("says null", "undecided", "says effect"))), 1))
  kable(data.frame(Test = sub(" \\|.*", "", rownames(shares)),
                   Truth = sub(".*\\| ", "", rownames(shares)), round(shares, 3),
                   check.names = FALSE, row.names = NULL),
        caption = "k = 20: share of datasets per answer (from study 06's cache).")
}
```

Under flat partial *r*, the share of true nulls that is confirmed is about the
same at *k* = 2 (.86) and *k* = 20 (.88). Under flat *R* it falls from .55 to
.06, under flat *R*² from .86 to .26, and under JZS from .54 to .30. Flat *R*
rarely calls a small effect null (.005 at *k* = 20) because it rarely calls
anything null: it leaves 92% of true nulls undecided. It finds a 0.1 effect
about as often as flat *R*² (.21) and JZS (.24), and more often than flat
partial *r* (.15); what it lacks is the ability to confirm nulls. Flat
partial *r*'s rates for small effects shift a little with *k*: the share of
0.1 effects it calls null rises from .52 to .60, and the share of 0.2 effects
it finds falls from .51 to .44. The joint tests of flat *R* and flat *R*² also
depend on how much variance the other predictors explain, the shared-scale
problem known as the conditional Lindley paradox (Som et al., 2016): their
log Bayes factor changes by −5.2 and −5.1 per unit of the others' *R*²,
against −0.5 for flat partial *r* (study 04).

## Only flat partial *r* is one coherent model {#sec-coherence}

A test of one coefficient is **coherent** when it equals the Bayes factor of
the full model against the same model with that coefficient's partial
correlation fixed at zero. That Bayes factor can be estimated from the full
model's posterior with the Savage–Dickey density ratio (Wagenmakers et al.,
2010). Under flat partial *r* the conditional test agrees with it to within a
factor of 1.10, on the 16 of 20 datasets where the ratio can be estimated
(the other four agree within three Monte Carlo standard errors). Under flat
*R*² the two diverge at *k* = 8, by a factor of up to 2.40 over its 19
estimable datasets (study 10, P4, the one failed check). This reflects the prior: its partial correlations are linked through
*R*², so information about the other coefficients shifts the evidence for
*x*₁.

Under flat *R*, the restricted model is not a proper alternative. When the
prior is conditioned on |ρ₁| < ε for shrinking ε (study 10, P7), the density of ρ₁
near zero keeps growing, and the *R*² of the other predictors goes to zero
(median .001 at *k* = 3 and .003 at *k* = 8, for ε = .005). The restricted
model therefore collapses to the intercept-only model. Under flat partial *r*
and flat *R*², the same restriction leaves a proper model (study 10, P6).

```{r}
#| fig-cap: "Study 10. The conditional and joint tests for x1 against the Savage-Dickey ratio of the joint model (flat partial r and flat R-squared)."
figure("10_coherence")
```

## Consistency when *k* grows with *n*

```{r}
#| fig-cap: "Study 08. Median log Bayes factor for the truth when k grows with n (pseudo-log scale)."
figure("08_growing_k")
```

All three priors are consistent when *k* grows with *n*, but the evidence
accumulates at very different speeds. For a true null with 500 predictors at
*n* = 2,000, the median log BF₀₁ is 407.6 under flat partial *r*, 3.7 under
flat *R*² and 1.9 under flat *R* (JZS: 149.3; Zellner–Siow: 410.8).

## Estimation and variable selection

Flat *R* and flat *R*² shrink the estimates more than flat partial *r*. This
lowers their prediction error with many predictors and a small sample: at
*k* = 8 and *n* = 30, their error is 0.37–0.77 and 0.42–0.75 times that of
ordinary least squares, against 0.72–0.81 for flat partial *r* (study 07). The
cost is bias in real effects (28% and 21% towards zero, against 8% for flat
partial *r*) and lower interval coverage (as low as .760 and .815, against
.916 or higher for flat partial *r*). In variable selection, flat partial *r*
behaves like Zellner–Siow: it includes few null predictors and misses more
real ones. Flat *R* and flat *R*² include more of both, while ranking the
predictors in nearly the same order (study 09).

# Discussion

We recommend flat partial *r*. Its test of one coefficient confirms true
nulls at the same rate at every number of predictors, its conditional test is
the Bayes factor of one coherent joint model, and its estimates are close to
unbiased with near-nominal interval coverage.

Our argument for preferring a stable rate of confirming nulls over the extra
caution of flat *R* is as follows. A default test should let the conclusion
about *x*₁ depend on the data about *x*₁. Under flat *R* and flat *R*², the
same data lead to a different verdict once covariates are added. That caution
is not learned from the data: the three conditional tests rank the datasets
identically, so the larger undecided share comes from the prior, which
shrinks each partial correlation as *k* grows (study 00), and not from weaker
evidence. A researcher who adds covariates would, under flat *R*, all but lose
the ability to confirm a null (.06 at *k* = 20) with nothing in the data to
show for it. Flat partial *r*'s own cost, described next, is visible and can
be reported.

The prior has three costs. First, with a small effect it leans towards the
null: at *k* = 20 it calls 60% of 0.1 effects null (averaged over *n* = 50 to
1,000). A
BF₀₁ above 3 from this prior therefore does not rule out a small effect, and
it is best reported together with the range of effects that the data cannot
distinguish from zero (the support curve in the package). Second, its
predictions are somewhat worse than those of flat *R* with many predictors
and a small sample. Third, it is conservative in variable selection.

The test itself is not new. A flat prior on one partial correlation is the
test of Kucharský et al. (2026) with α = 1, and the joint prior is LKJ(1)
(Lewandowski et al., 2009), which is also `stan_lm` with η = 1. Two points were
not found in the literature searched. The first is that this test is the
Bayes factor of one joint model, and that no such model exists under flat
*R*, both in the sense of compatibility by conditioning, the notion the
Savage–Dickey ratio assumes (marginalisation and projection are the
alternatives; Consonni & Veronese, 2008). The second is that, for the conditional tests, the drift of *R*-based and
*R*²-based defaults with *k* changes where the test decides and leaves what it
can detect unchanged. Their joint tests are a different matter: with
correlated predictors they separate nulls from small effects worse than JZS
(an AUC difference of −.064 at *k* = 2 and correlation .70). The search was
not a systematic review.

The study has four limitations. All results are simulations, limited to the
designs studied. The criteria are checked numerically, not proven. There is
no reanalysis of real data. Finally, there is no evidence yet on which prior
matches how explained variance grows with the number of predictors in
published regressions.
